problem: Prior RL-based object-goal navigation couples navigation ability with target features (word embedding or visual feature of the goal) in the state, so unseen target classes give out-of-distribution states and generalization to new targets is poor. Prior zero-shot methods such as SSNet also depend on the similarity between test and train targets.
motivation: Real environments contain countless object classes, so training an agent on every one is infeasible and zero-shot object navigation matters. The authors argue that class-specific features in the state are the reason for poor zero-shot transfer, so the state should carry no class or environment features.
key_idea: Build a class-independent state from detection boxes, each described only by its semantic similarity to the goal and its spatial position, sorted by similarity, and process it with a GCN and LSTM actor-critic policy, which decouples navigation skill from target identity.
insight: Because objects are identified only by their relative similarity to the goal, and not by class or appearance, test-time states for unseen goals and scenes look like training states. This is why the test-class SR (66.9) can approach or exceed the train-class SR (63.4) in Table 1, while SSNet reaches only 28.6 on test classes. The cross-scene tables show the same effect, for example kitchen to bedroom test-class SR of 46.4 vs 3.6 for SSNet. No ablation of the GCN or the sorting is reported, so their individual contributions are untested.
method: State representation: a 20x5 matrix with one row per detected object, r=[h, s, xc, yc, area], where h marks the target and s is the similarity to the target. Rows are sorted by s in descending order, the top 20 are kept, and the rest are zero-padded. No visual features are used.
Semantic similarity: cosine similarity between the word embedding of each object and that of the navigation target, so objects are identified only relative to the target.
GCN module: treats objects as graph nodes with similarity and spatial features, and learns object relationships and layout over several graph convolution layers.
Policy network: an LSTM keeps action history, followed by an actor-critic head that outputs the policy, trained with policy gradient (A3C-style).
Reward: +5 on success, with a bonus growing with the cosine similarity of the objects in view, and -0.01 when no object is in view (following SSNet).
Detections: ground-truth detection results are used, as in other works, so the zero-shot range depends on the detector.

setting.backbone: GCN + LSTM + actor-critic (trained from scratch); word embeddings for similarity
setting.training_data: AI2-THOR, 80 train scenes (kitchen, living room, bedroom, bathroom; 20 train and 10 test scenes per type) with 18 or 14 train target classes out of 22. The cross-scene settings train on kitchen only or living room only.
setting.observation: Egocentric RGB, used only through ground-truth object detection boxes (position, area, similarity to target)
setting.action_space: Discrete: MoveAhead, RotateLeft, RotateRight, LookDown, LookUp, Done
setting.privileged: Ground-truth object detections are used as input at test time

numbers_note: Benchmarks are custom AI2-THOR splits following SSNet, not canonical ones. Only L>=1 test-class numbers are listed; L>=5 and train-class numbers are also in the tables. Table numbering for the cross-scene tables is inferred from order (captions are all labeled tab1).
results: CIRN reaches test-class SR of 66.9 (18/4) and 64.4 (14/8), against SSNet's 28.6 and 21.5. In the harder cross-scene, cross-target settings it reaches 46.4 to 80.4 SR, while SSNet stays at 3.6 to 10.8.
limitations: Uses ground-truth object detections, so real-world performance depends on the detector and the zero-shot range is limited to its vocabulary.

Evaluated only in AI2-THOR against a single baseline (SSNet), with no ablation of the GCN or sorting and no real-robot tests. SPL is low in unfamiliar scenes, and performance in complex scenes like the kitchen lags.
